title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents
authors: Jiaru Zou, Yunzhe Qi, Sirui Chen et al.
abstract: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. title: SkillScaffold: Scaffolding Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Policy-Adaptive Skill Credit Assignment and Selective Injection
authors: Wenlin Zhong, Hao Wang, Kun Yuan et al.
abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from multi-turn interactions with verifiable outcomes. Textual skills can improve exploration by distilling prior interactions into reusable guidance. However, existing skill-based RL approaches often either assume skill injection is beneficial or rely on indirect feedback or rollout-intensive evaluation to assess its utility. Our pilot studies show that rollout-based utility estimation for skill credit assignment

title: SEAR: Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics
authors: Xinyi Wang, Bangzheng Li, Hanyu Wang et al.
abstract: Frontier language-model agents can now improve robots on their own: they write control code, test it, and keep what works as skills and memories for the next task. We introduce SEAR (Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics), a framework and benchmark built around two questions. Is the agent really learning, or just trying more often? title: BLADE: Auditing Information Use for Failure Attribution in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Xiaoguang Guo, Yaohao Long, Chuxu Zhang
abstract: Large language model multi-agent systems extend individual agents' capabilities through collaboration across specialized roles, tools, and workflows. Yet collaboration makes failures harder to diagnose: one agent may misinterpret a correct result while others carry the mistake forward. Failure attribution therefore seeks to identify the responsible agent and decisive error step. title: Beyond the Verdict: Agentic Code Judging with Verifiable Feedback
authors: Zheye Deng, Sha Li, Changlong Yu et al.
abstract: Test-time scaling for large language models (LLMs) can involve generating multiple candidate solutions for selection or revising an earlier attempt. To guide selection and revision, we need a verifier that can estimate candidate correctness and provide evidence of failure. In competitive programming, however, official judging systems provide authoritative verdicts under finite submission budgets, without revealing failure explanations or failing inputs. title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning
authors: Bowen Ding, Mingda Wan, Yuhan Chen et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) agents, yet efficient critic-free algorithms (e.g., GRPO) suffer from a fundamental uniform credit assignment dilemma that broadcasts trajectory-level advantages equally to all actions. title: Knowledge Graphs as Files: An Agent Harness Where Tool Creation and Tool Use Co-Evolve
authors: Yuyang Bai, Yu Wang, Yu Zhang
abstract: Searching text-rich knowledge graphs requires following relations while examining textual evidence. Predefined graph interfaces constrain what evidence agents can access, even when they write code to combine tool calls or process retrieved subgraphs. We propose direct knowledge graph interaction (DKGI), a harness in which language model agents create graph access tools directly over complete node and edge files. The agent writes Python code to follow relations, combine node sets, and select text

title: Can an Agent Learn to Predict Its Own Failure? Outcome-Grounded Confidence Calibration in LLM Agents
authors: Ashutosh Hathidara
abstract: Controlling an acting LLM agent means deciding, at each step of a long-horizon task, whether to trust its next action, abstain, or hand off to a human. That decision needs a per-step confidence signal predicting whether the current rollout will eventually succeed. The agent's own self-reported verbalized confidence is the natural candidate, but existing reinforcement learning methods calibrate it against the correctness of a decision at the current step. title: LLM Agents for Automated Post-Training via Structured Recipe Optimization
authors: Ruohong Liu, Bohan Tang, Lekang Jiang et al.
abstract: Automated post-training transforms pre-trained large language models (LLMs) into models capable of handling diverse domains by automatically constructing and optimizing a recipe of coupled decisions over data sources, data processing, cross-domain composition, and training configuration under a limited experimental budget. Existing automation either searches predefined recipe spaces that enable systematic optimization but remain fixed rather than adapting their available choices to the target ta

title: Lost in Implicit Routing: How LLM Agents Fail to Load Relevant Skills at Scale
authors: Jinlin Liu, Wei Chen, Xiaojin Zhang
abstract: Reusable skills let LLM agents load task-specific instructions on demand, but they make execution depend on implicit routing over skill metadata. We test whether this design scales by holding SkillsBench tasks and their golden skills fixed while adding irrelevant skills. We find skill routing collapse: agents increasingly load fewer or no skills, even though the relevant skills remain available. title: Judges Follow the Reference: The Derivation Gap in Verifying Tool-Call Arguments
authors: Linhai Ma, Yan Wang, Lingfei Qian et al.
abstract: Tool-call judges evaluate argument values proposed by LLM agents. We find that they accept a correct value less often when their input holds no reference for it, that is, no text that says what the value should be. This happens when the value is a default value from the function schema that the user did not mention, when it has to be inferred, or when the text it comes from was cut from the judge input. title: Reliable Memory from Unstable Growth: Curating Self-Written Agent Playbooks with Randomized Experiments
authors: Hoang Pham, Cong-Duy Nguyen, Dong Le et al.
abstract: Persistent textual memory lets language-model agents reuse lessons from past tasks to improve on future multi-step tasks without retraining. Systems such as ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet keep it as a playbook: lessons the agent writes after each task and reads in its prompt. A key challenge is to decide which lessons improve later tasks. title: Receiver Decides Agent-to-Agent Negotiations
authors: Fardeen Sadab, Alif Hasnain, Afsana Shehrin et al.
abstract: When one language-model agent asks another for money, which of the two decides how much changes hands? We ran a round-robin tournament of 1,049 negotiations among fifteen agents. In each game a requester tries to raise money from a holder that has been told to keep a $100 endowment. Knowing which agent holds the money explains 47% of the variance in the amount transferred; knowing which agent asks explains 2%. Dropping the most extreme agents narrows the split to 22% against 4%. title: Delegating Earth science model calibration to knowledge-guided LLM agents
authors: Zhanliang Zhu, Ziwei Li, Liujun Zhu et al.
abstract: Applying process-based Earth science models to new sites and questions often requires expert calibration decisions. Reliable delegation to language-model agents must preserve scientific competence and reproducibility. Here we develop a general calibration harness (GCH) for end-to-end delegation from a calibration request to assessed results. title: Choosing LLMs for Strategic Agent Interactions
authors: Arastun Mammadli, Herbert Woisetschläger, Jawad Fayaz et al.
abstract: Game-theoretic benchmarks claim that large language model (LLM) strategic decision-making varies across game types, interaction structures, and capability dimensions. However, they only evaluate strategic performance across individual fixed models. In parallel, contemporary LLM routers pick models under quality-cost trade-offs, but with no notion of a strategic structure. They do not account for an opponent that might be unknown, and that can adapt over time and shift the feedback signal. To add

title: SimInter: Evidence-Grounded User Simulation with Interview-Based Profile Enrichment for Conversational Recommender Systems
authors: Erfan Shahabi, Amirhossein Roshandel, Mohammad Sadegh Sadeghi et al.
abstract: Conversational Recommender Systems (CRSs) require reliable user simulators for cost-effective evaluation. LLM-based simulators have made realistic simulation possible but typically condition on profiles derived from explicit ratings, demographics, and static sources capturing surface preferences while omitting implicit behavioral characteristics such as decision-making style, aspect-level preferences, and domain expertise. title: Output Discipline Sets the Floor: A Falsification-Guided, Model-Agnostic Agent Protocol for Auditable Hypothesis-Driven Decision Making
authors: Jing Liu, Yongxing Qi, Ping Yao et al.
abstract: What binds large language models on auditable, hypothesis-driven decision tasks, where every candidate can be checked against the evidence? On the public TCMEval-SDT benchmark for Traditional Chinese Medicine syndrome differentiation (200 cases), the binding constraint is output discipline and reasoning structure, not model capability alone: two years of model scaling move zero-shot scores by only -0.03 to +0.08, while output-discipline failures (non-terminating reasoning, format non-compliance,

title: Encrypted Skills Can Become New Security Exploits If AI Agents Know How to Decipher
authors: Yan-Lun Chen, Pin-Yu Chen, Chia-Mu Yu
abstract: Third-party skills can expose LLM agents to malicious instructions hidden by encoding. We introduce Ciphered Skill Injection (CSI), which embeds such instructions in skill files for agents to decode and follow. We evaluate Caesar and layered variants across eight models and 139 injection-task pairs, separating instruction recovery from attack success. title: Beyond Answer Sharing: TrueMAD for Targeted Peer Engagement in Multi-Agent Debate
authors: Dezheng Bao, Sihang Du, Renhong Huang et al.
abstract: Multi-agent debate (MAD) aims to improve large language model reasoning by exposing agents to alternative solutions and enabling iterative revision. However, standard broadcast-style MAD makes peer answers visible without requiring agents to engage with a particular peer claim. As a result, reliable reasoning may be suppressed by conflicting or majority responses, limiting achievable performance, while erroneous reasoning may persist and degrade final predictions without actionable feedback. title: TextualRL: Textual Reinforcement Learning for Context Management
authors: Tianyu Huai, Jie Zhou, Bo Mao et al.
abstract: LLM agents can adapt to task feedback by revising the textual context that guides their behavior, without changing their model parameters. However, turning execution rewards into reusable context updates is challenging: individual trajectories offer limited comparative evidence about what to change, while task-specific fixes may overgeneralize when incorporated into a shared context. title: Fan Out or Relay? Ownership-Aware Routing for LLM Agents Querying Siloed Tables
authors: Zhexi Feng
abstract: Inside organizations, a question's data often sit with several owners, who query their own tables but never hand them over. An LLM coordinator can fan out, sending the question to every owner at once, or relay, querying owners in turn and reusing earlier rows. We show that neither is safe in advance, because data ownership decides which one is right. title: AM-Bench: Understanding Agents under Task Underspecification across Models and Harnesses
authors: Kaiyu Huang, Yiting Li, Angyang Gu et al.
abstract: Ambiguous or incomplete task specifications complicate both execution and clarification for language-model agents. Yet agents' responses to these information gaps remain poorly characterized across models and execution harnesses. We present AM-Bench, a benchmark built from 48 tasks adapted from Terminal-Bench 2.0 and Harness-Bench. title: Can Agents Forget When Asked? A Benchmark for Memory Unlearning in LLM Agents
authors: Bofan Xie, Chaokun Wang, Guanchen Ge et al.
abstract: Long-term memory has become a core component of large language model (LLM) agents. As agents accumulate personal information over long-term use, users increasingly ask them to delete sensitive or outdated facts. A memory system should honor such requests. It should remove exactly what was requested and keep the rest of its memory intact. title: Cost-Efficient Privacy Enforcement for Email-Generating LLM Agents under Strategic Information Requests
authors: Qikun Cai, Tao Huang, Chen Hou
abstract: LLM agents now act as delegated communication intermediaries: they read private context, draft messages, and send externally visible emails on behalf of a user. Existing checker-repair defenses can reduce inappropriate disclosure, but they rely on repeated calls to a remote action LLM (the model that drafts and repairs the email) and a remote checker LLM whenever a draft fails validation. title: Agent-Reflex: Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively
authors: Guanting Dong, Xinyu Yang, Jiajie Jin et al.
abstract: Large language models have evolved from single-turn chatbots into interactive agents capable of long-horizon reasoning. In real deployments, MCP tool services can return noisy feedback and users may intervene to correct the agent, but existing methods provide limited supervision for reflection learning and failure recovery. To bridge this gap, we propose Agent-Reflex, a general training framework for incentivizing proactive reflection in agents. Specifically, Agent-Reflex comprises three stages.

title: Training LLMs for Multi-Agent Collaboration with Verifiable Information Rewards
authors: Keru Chen, Sen Lin, Yingbin Liang et al.
abstract: Effective collaboration among large language model (LLM) agents in multi-agent systems requires sharing relevant evidence, requesting missing information, and incorporating teammates' contributions into decisions. Training these behaviors is challenging because final task outcomes provide limited feedback on the value of individual messages. title: ECMR: Evidence-Aware Deliberation Control for Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning
authors: Yuan Liu, Haoyue Peng, Fanliang Hu et al.
abstract: Multi-agent Large Language Model (LLM) systems typically commit to a deliberation protocol before inference. A fixed protocol cannot allocate computation differently to resolved and unresolved instances, and it may mistake repeated support for independent confirmation. We study this failure as semantic false consensus: a confident group answer supported by narrow, duplicated, or correlated rationales. title: RT-J: Large-Scale Pretraining of Relational Transformers for Context-Efficient Predictions
authors: Rishabh Ranjan, Vignesh Kothapalli, Harshvardhan Agarwal et al.
abstract: Foundation models for tables and relational databases are increasingly used for predictive tasks across various scientific and industrial domains. However, adapting existing models to unseen datasets requires tens of thousands of examples. Here we introduce RT-J, an 85M-parameter relational foundation model (RFM) that makes accurate predictions even with hundreds of in-context examples or fewer. title: Socratic Skill Learning: Interleaving Teaching and Practice for Transferable Agent Skills
authors: Letian Zhu, Han Li, Yifan Yao et al.
abstract: Agent Skills improve LLM agents by making task knowledge reusable across sessions. Learning transferable Skills requires evidence about a procedure and its conditions of use, which a successful task attempt can leave untested. We introduce Socratic Skill Learning (SSL), which interleaves expert teaching with Student practice. title: ProtoArena: Can AI Agents Discover and Exploit Real-World Cross-Component Protocol Vulnerabilities?
authors: Fasheng Miao, Zhaoyu Hu, Xiang Li et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for vulnerability analysis, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of exploitation that depends on interactions among network protocol components. Such vulnerabilities arise from inconsistencies in message interpretation, timing, state, or trust assumptions across participants. title: Agentic-MatriBO: Capability-Compiled Agentic Bayesian Optimization for Materials and Chemical Design
authors: Yu Zeng, Yuchuan Chen, Ziyue Zhang et al.
abstract: Materials and chemical optimization must choose the next synthesis, characterization, or high-fidelity simulation from sequential observations under a limited budget. Large language models can use task knowledge to propose adjustments, but composing surrogates, acquisition functions, and search strategies is constrained by compatibility, parameter dependencies, and evidence requirements. title: Empowering Edge Agents: A Systematic Analysis of Edge-Cloud Collaboration in LLM Agent Execution
authors: Pengcheng Huang, Zhenghao Liu, Shixin Ren et al.
abstract: Edge-cloud collaboration combines the lower inference overhead and greater data locality of edge-side execution with the stronger capabilities of cloud-hosted models. However, as LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon scenarios, cloud participation becomes interleaved throughout execution rather than a one-shot decision for each query. title: Agentic4PDM: Host-Governed Evidence Admissibility for Industrial Fault Diagnosis
authors: Nam V. Nguyen, Hoang Van Truong, Hieu D. D. et al.
abstract: We study industrial fault diagnosis as a classification task that assigns sensor time-series windows to predefined health states or fault types. Scarce labels and changing operating conditions make repeated training of specialized classifiers costly. Yet structures such as periodicity, trends, and transients can remain diagnostically informative and be examined through reusable analytical tools. title: Instructions Are Evidence, Not Objectives: Measuring Outcome Alignment of Agents
authors: Kaiming Liu, Yuxuan Liu, Jinrui Ju et al.
abstract: Large language model agents can follow complex human instructions to solve real-world tasks. In practice, however, initial instructions are often incomplete. In our analysis of 100 user-agent trajectories from SWE-chat, 56\% of initial instructions omit requirements that later emerge as necessary, and 52\% of the useful follow-up requirements could have been inferred from the project. title: Degrees of Freedom in Multi-Agent Coordination: Between Centralized and Decentralized Regimes
authors: Yiqing Peng, Hehai Lin, Zixuan Wang et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) are commonly organized around two coordination regimes. Centralized coordination provides explicit control but can create a bottleneck at a single coordination locus, whereas decentralized coordination offers local autonomy but must achieve effective collaboration through distributed decisions and experience. title: TSRL: Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning for Continual Agent Training
authors: Yuqian Fu, Kaiwen Jiang, Zijun Song et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents excel at complex, multi-step tasks but suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual learning--acquiring new skills often degrades previously mastered capabilities. Existing post-training paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is sample-efficient but prone to severe forgetting, while Reinforcement Learning (RL) preserves prior capabilities but converges slowly without expert guidance. title: Upstream Influence, Downstream Re-Anchoring in LLM Agent Chains
authors: Chun-Yu Hsu, Lun-Wei Ku, Chung-Chi Chen
abstract: People act on evaluative judgments produced by LLM agents, and in multi-agent systems those judgments pass through several agents before reaching a person. We show that a workflow's information architecture---source access, handoff format, and which model reads the untrusted content---governs how much of a coordinated manipulation reaches the end. title: Can Agents Truly Forget? Explore Machine Unlearning for LLM Agents
authors: Junkai Lin, Ge Xu, Zheng Xu et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown strong capabilities in interactive problem solving, tool use, and long-horizon task execution. However, they may also acquire sensitive or private knowledge during training and expose it during deployment. Retraining a model from scratch to remove such knowledge is prohibitively costly, making machine unlearning a more practical approach. title: Executable Prefix Values for Locating Agent Failures
authors: Bingyu Shen, Jiaqi Tang, Lan Wei et al.
abstract: Work on debugging LLM agents treats the "first mistake" marked by a human or LLM judge as ground truth for where a trajectory failed. We ask whether such labels point at causes or symptoms, and make the distinction executable: we restart the agent from reconstructed intermediate states of a failed trajectory and estimate its prefix value V(h_t), the probability of success from each step, with a certified point of no return (PNR) for a failure. title: MAS-Gate: Unlocking Multi-Agent System Lifecycle via Node-Centric Quantification
authors: Hehai Lin, Zixuan Wang, Ming Yan et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) can solve complex problems beyond the reach of a single agent by decomposing tasks and coordinating complementary capabilities. Despite extensive research on MAS, existing work largely focuses on specific aspects or individual phases of their development and operation, resulting in fragmented perspectives with objectives and signals that are difficult to reconcile across these different settings. To bridge these disconnected perspectives

title: Many Steps into One: Reasoning Contraction and the Limits of Safe Memory Reuse for LLM Agents
authors: Jianghong Zhou, Hao Rong, Chen Lin et al.
abstract: Thought templates, skill libraries, agent memories and caches turn many reasoning steps into one. We call this reasoning contraction. A contracted memory saves reasoning steps and errors until its facts change, then quietly answers wrong. Most systems trust memories by counting successes and failures. title: Teacher-Guided Tool Learning for Small Language Models via Bidirectional KL Constraints
authors: Haoxuan Gao, Qin-Wen Luo, Xiang Chen et al.
abstract: External tools can extend the capabilities of small language models (SLMs), enabling their deployment in resource constrained environments. However, their limited capabilities make it difficult for SLMs to discover effective tool use behaviors through reinforcement learning alone, while direct teacher supervision suffers from teacher student behavioral distribution mismatch and may propagate erroneous preferences. title: Coupled Harness--Model Evolution for Scientific Equation Discovery
authors: Pengze Li, Jiaquan Zhang, Encheng Su et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to discover scientific equations from experimental data. Such a discovery system has two parts that must work together: a library of executable computational tools and the model's tool-use policy. The tools supply the solving capability, from diagnosing structure in the data to fitting candidate equations; the policy plans and orchestrates their use. title: DoubtLess: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Efficient Reasoning
authors: Minghao Luo, Liang Chen
abstract: Reasoning models achieve strong performance through long chains of thought (CoT), but often spend more tokens than needed to solve a problem. Existing ways to shorten the CoT require additional training for each model, add a fixed steering vector to the model's hidden states, or use decoding heuristics such as stopping early or banning words like "wait", which can reduce accuracy. title: OmniCompass: A Holistic Benchmark for Omni-Modal Video Grounding and Understanding
authors: Xuyang Liu, Shihao Wang, Xinyu Wei et al.
abstract: With the rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), evaluating their video understanding capabilities has become increasingly important. Existing video understanding benchmarks cover only part of the evaluation dimensions, limiting systematic diagnosis of omni-modal video understanding. title: GeoReader: Learning Latent Geometry for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
authors: Rong Li, Shijie Li, Jiangyong Huang et al.
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with metric and multi-view relationships that remain implicit in RGB observations. Geometry foundation models recover this structure from RGB, but existing methods either fuse the estimated features with visual tokens and learn to use them from question answering alone, or align VLM latents with geometry features. title: DTScribe: Generating Models for Digital Twin Reporting using Local Large Language Models
authors: Kérian Fiter, Angelica Portocarrero, Bentley Oakes
abstract: The development of a digital twin brings together many stakeholders and technical components. We have previously investigated the reporting of the conceptual architecture for these digital twins as an artifact for discussion. However, we find that the activity of modeling the digital twin for visualization and consensus-building can be quite tedious and time-consuming. title: Jev-ToM: Evaluating Theory of Mind in Typed Decision Models
authors: Kawai Chung, Chunkit Chan, Yuxuan Liu et al.
abstract: Dialogue and collaborative assistants repeatedly judge what a partner knows, believes, or intends. Typed decision models offer a potential alternative to generative large language models for bounded Theory of Mind (ToM) selection. We present Jev-ToM, comparing five typed decision models and seven generative baselines on 11,117 English text questions from nine ToM benchmarks across six capability groups. title: Beyond Answer Voting: Fine-Grained Correction of LLM Reasoning through Graph Alignment across Sampled Traces
authors: Haotian Liu, Yingjian Chen, Xiaohang Xu et al.
abstract: Large language models increasingly tackle tasks that require multi-step reasoning, where errors in intermediate claims can affect the final answer. Self-consistency (SC) improves reasoning by voting over sampled final answers, but its vote leaves intermediate disagreements unresolved. To address this problem, we introduce DDRG (Disagreement-Driven Verification Guided by Reasoning Graphs), a framework for selective correction from a frozen bank of reasoning traces. authors: Zhouhan Zhong, Qiuhong Shen, Xingyi Yang et al.
abstract: 3D part assembly aims to reconstruct a complete shape from a set of unassembled parts by predicting a rigid SE(3) transformation for each part. Because the placement of a part is rarely determined by its own geometry, the task demands reasoning over the entire part set, and existing methods, which rely on pairwise relations or iterative generation and verification, scale poorly to objects with many parts. title: Efficient Safety Guardrails through Latent Dual-Hypothesis Reasoning with On-Demand Trace Reconstruction
authors: Md Asiful Islam, Fahmida Alam, Mihai Surdeanu
abstract: Guardrail approaches that rely on reasoning-based large language models (LLM) improve safety decisions, but come with substantial inference overhead due to the explicit reasoning. We introduce LR-Guard (Latent Reasoning Guardrail), an efficient and explainable guardrail that jointly learns structured latent reasoning and on-demand reasoning reconstruction. title: Chain of Thought Monitoring Can Fail Even When CoT Is Necessary
authors: Lennart Bürger, Piotr Komorowski, Moritz Weckbecker et al.
abstract: Chain of Thought (CoT) monitoring is used by frontier labs to detect misbehaviour of AI systems. Yet, its reliability remains poorly understood. We attribute this to the lack of a successful organizing principle that leads to generalizable conclusions about monitoring reliability in different regimes. authors: Gonzalo Mancera, Julian Fierrez, Aythami Morales et al.
abstract: This work investigates the application of the Membership Inference Test (MINT) to large language models (LLMs) fine-tuned with LoRA, aiming to determine whether specific samples were used during training and address concerns about data privacy, leakage, and transparency. title: HaloBlock: Faster and Better Decoding for Diffusion Large Language Models
authors: Zhaohui Zheng, Chenhang He, Jinrui Zhang et al.
abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have attracted increasing research attention due to their bidirectional attention and arbitrary order decoding. However, there are two issues in dLLMs inference: the decoding difficulty is dominated by the tokens on the right side of the block, and the block-wise decoding inherently suffers from boundary contextual discontinuity. title: PaceReasoner: Label-Free Learning to Answer Briefly from Long Reasoning
authors: Changguo Jia, Zhiyou Xiao, Xinbei Ma et al.
abstract: Extended chain-of-thought reasoning improves problem-solving performance but increases inference cost and latency, motivating more accurate answers with shorter reasoning. We introduce PaceReasoner, a label-free test-time reinforcement learning framework that uses a model's LONG responses to improve its SHORT-mode accuracy. title: Checking the Checkers: A Synthesis of Verifier Noise and Robustness in RLVR
authors: Savyasachi Gupta, Aniruddha Srinivas Joshi
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a principal recipe for improving the reasoning of large language models (LLMs). It rests on the assumption that the checker scoring each response is itself correct. In practice, rule-based checkers reject correct answers in unexpected formats, unit tests accept incorrect programs, and LLM judges can be led to approve empty or adversarial responses. This work surveys 58 studies that measure, analyze, or mitigate such verifier errors

title: Dynamic K-Head: Difficulty-Supervised Budget Selection for Continuous Latent Reasoning
authors: Ying Li, Yuqi Chen, Sixuan Li et al.
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) improves reasoning but incurs substantial autoregressive rationale cost. Continuous CoT moves intermediate computation into recurrent hidden states, yet typically uses a fixed number of updates even though the best budget varies across questions and accuracy need not improve monotonically with $K$. We introduce Dynamic K-Head, a question-conditioned, pre-rollout budget selector. It is jointly trained with the reasoner under selected budgets, using difficulty supervision ba

title: The Image Still Has a Say: Final-Answer Repair for Multimodal Chain-of-Thought
authors: Yulan Pan, Xiaoyu Xu, Zhihong Shen
abstract: Although chain-of-thought prompting has improved multimodal reasoning, it is still difficult to produce correct final answers, as the reasoning can drift away from the image. Besides, the trace is already fixed when the answer is generated, leaving no room for self-correction. Considering the image is still available at the final-answer step, we think it is reasonable to fix the answer there without rewriting the reasoning. As such, the problem becomes to correct the final answer using the image

title: Facts Don't Speak Louder than Words: The Behavioral Essence of Long-CoT Distillation
authors: Yongcan Yu, Jian Liang, Lingxiao He et al.
abstract: While long chain-of-thought (CoT) distillation significantly improves the reasoning abilities of language models, its underlying mechanism remains poorly understood. Current pipelines generally rely on rejection sampling to gather reasoning traces across diverse prompts, assuming that factual correctness and broad problem coverage are indispensable. Surprisingly, we find that training exclusively on flawed reasoning trajectories or a restricted prompt set yields nearly comparable performance. Dr

title: DPOison-VL: Clean Preference Poisoning in Vision-Language Direct Preference Optimization
authors: Chengtao Jian, Kai Yang
abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has become a widely adopted approach for aligning vision-language models (VLMs), yet the security of multimodal preference data remains largely unexplored. Existing preference poisoning attacks either corrupt explicit supervision signals or require visible triggers, making them detectable under human inspection. We introduce DPOison-VL, the first clean preference poisoning attack against VLM-DPO, which manipulates model alignment solely through imperceptible

title: Rethinking Projector Training in Multimodal LLMs
authors: Fabian Gröger, Naël Ouerghemi, Shuo Wen et al.
abstract: Multimodal LLMs are typically trained by first aligning a vision encoder with a language model via projector training on large image-caption datasets, followed by joint training of the full multimodal model. Despite its widespread use, the role of the projector training stage remains poorly understood. We find that (i) using only $10$ to $20\%$ of the data for training the projector already recovers most downstream performance gains, and (ii) projectors trained on different datasets can be linea

title: EgoOmniWorld: Unifying Egocentric Understanding via Ego-Action-World Interactions
authors: Songruo Chen, Yuqian Fu, Yu Li et al.
abstract: Egocentric video understanding spans diverse capabilities, modalities, and evaluation formats, yet these are often studied in isolation despite their tight coupling in real-world interaction. We propose the Ego-Action-World interaction loop as a unifying principle: the wearer perceives the world, forms goals, acts, changes the world, and uses feedback to guide subsequent behavior. Based on this view, we introduce EgoOmniWorld, a benchmark organized around four complementary interaction structure

title: Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations by Correcting Modality Misrouting in Omnimodal LLMs
authors: Yu Mi, Licheng Pan, Jiayi Zhu et al.
abstract: Omnimodal large language models (OLLMs) are susceptible to cross-modal hallucinations under audio-visual interference. We find that, for a substantial fraction of incorrect joint predictions, the question-relevant unimodal branch can still recover the correct answer, suggesting that task-relevant evidence can remain recoverable from the relevant modality even when it is not reflected in the joint prediction. We refer to this recoverable failure pattern as \emph{modality misrouting}. We propose C

title: MERIT: Multimodal Evidence Reasoning over Image Tables
authors: Haoyang Jiang, Zhuotong Fan, Mingyang Yi et al.
abstract: Table reasoning with language models typically assumes access to clean textual tables. In practice, tables are often serialized into text, which can corrupt cell contents, distort structural relationships, and discard visual cues, leaving the model to reason over incomplete evidence. In contrast, table images retain this information, but using it requires both accurate perception and reasoning grounded in the relevant cells. To address this, we propose MERIT (Multimodal Evidence Reasoning over I

title: MMTA: Benchmarking Multimodal Temporal Analysis with Time Series, Text, and Vision
authors: Ziyang Zhang, Shenyi Li, Yilin Wang et al.
abstract: Time-series analysis is increasingly studied in multimodal settings, yet most benchmarks pair temporal signals with text or with visualizations derived from the same signal. This leaves open whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can integrate time series with real-world visual evidence. We introduce MMTA (multimodal temporal analysis), a benchmark of tri-modal tasks with diverse cross-modal complementarity patterns among time series, text, and vision. MMTA spans nine domains -- roboti

title: Safety for Whom? Benchmarking Understanding Beyond Refusal in Egocentric Multimodal Assistants
authors: Yewon Han, Jisu Jeon, Suhyun Choi et al.
abstract: Egocentric multimodal assistants see through the user's eyes and guide what the user does next, so their outputs directly shape physical actions, including those that affect bystanders. Yet existing safety evaluations do not distinguish whom a response would harm, and score only whether a model refuses. Pooling all harms into one refusal rate hides two failures: a model may protect one target but not another, and it may refuse without understanding the risk, or understand it and comply anyway. W

title: Do Factuality Methods Make LLMs More Factual? Reproducibility and Fair Comparison
authors: Pratuat Amatya, Vinay Setty, V Venktesh et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to human preferences, after pre-training and supervised fine-tuning steps. However, standard RL alignment steps such as RLHF do not focus on factuality of LLMs, hence they may generate non-factual information, which could result in unintended consequences. In response, a number of factuality alignment approaches have been proposed in the literature which claim to improve factuality of LLMs on their own benchmarks. However, these methods have not been repr

title: Cross-Lingual Transfer of Evil Vectors Is Directionally Asymmetric
authors: Juann Kim, Minku Kang
abstract: Persona vectors are linear directions in the residual-stream activations of LLMs that encode behavioral traits and enable fine-grained control over model behavior. Among them, the evil persona vector is particularly relevant to understanding harmful behavior, jailbreak vulnerabilities, and the unlearning of harmful knowledge. Yet whether this vector reflects a genuinely cross-lingual concept, rather than an artifact of its extraction language, remains untested. We conduct a systematic evil-vecto

title: Where Words Begin and End
authors: Husein Zolkepli
abstract: Forced aligners locate each word of a known transcript in the audio, and many speech pipelines depend on them. In our own data, a widely used CTC aligner inserts a pause at nearly every word boundary, and we found almost no aligner evaluated on telephone audio. We compare nine aligner configurations against human word boundaries on read, conversational and telephone English. title: MFG: Multi-turn Feedback Guided Molecular Optimization
authors: Trieu Nguyen, Frazier N. Baker, Ruoxi Gao et al.
abstract: Multi-objective molecular optimization is a critical process in drug discovery that aims to modify a given molecule to simultaneously improve multiple properties while maintaining a similar overall structure. This process often requires iterative modifications guided by computational or experimental feedback. Recent large language model (LLM)-based methods have begun to explore this iterative approach; however, these methods are not explicitly trained to leverage such feedback, while existing ap

title: Bayesian Test-Time Inference of Task-Aligned Similarity from Weak Interactive Feedback
authors: Weida Liang, Kenji Kawaguchi
abstract: Language model systems repeatedly make test-time decisions by comparing similarity: they retrieve exemplars, rank candidates, and revise responses. Yet similarity is not unique: lexical, semantic, structural, and stylistic resemblance can point to different candidates, and the task-aligned notion can change across instances. title: To Align or Not To Align: Check Your COMPASS Before You Train
authors: Fabian Gröger, Petar Damjanović, Maria Brbić
abstract: Combining pretrained models is a common strategy for building AI systems, whether by aligning a vision encoder with a language model or merging fine-tuned checkpoints. However, finding compatible pairs typically requires costly empirical search, as compatibility is known only after alignment or merging. We propose COMPASS (COMPatibility ASsessment Score), a theoretically motivated diagnostic that estimates whether a model pair will be compatible prior to alignment or merging. Building on the obs

title: Empathy Is Not the Scapegoat for Declines in Factuality and Reliability
authors: Letian Shi, Kanwal Mehreen, Deheng Zhang et al.
abstract: Language models are increasingly expected to support users in stressful or uncertain situations, where warmth and empathy are desirable. While recent work associates warmer models with reduced reliability, we show that this conclusion is incomplete. Prior studies often train primarily on empathetic dialogue, making it difficult to separate tone effects from SFT-induced distribution shift. We revisit this issue at both the model and evaluation levels. We study prompting, SFT, and RL for inducing

title: MemoryVLN: From Ego-Aware Memory Representation to Cross-Context Memory Reuse in Vision-Language Navigation
authors: Xueyao Wei, Yifei Wang, Delun Li et al.
abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have shown strong potential for embodied vision-language navigation (VLN), yet their performance degrades on long-horizon trajectories due to context-length limits, redundant historical observations, and unstable spatial alignment across time. These issues make it difficult to both compress long navigation histories and reliably reuse past spatial experience. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{MemoryVLN}, a unified memory-driven navigation syste

title: Not All Drift Is a Mechanism: Tracing Prompt Adaptation in LLMs
authors: Mikhail Aleksandrov, Nail Bashirov, Maksim Ivanov et al.
abstract: Prompt-based adaptation offers several ways to specialize a frozen language model, ranging from natural-language prompt optimization to learned continuous prompts. These methods are usually compared through downstream performance, although similar outputs need not arise from similar internal computations. We study how discrete prompt optimization, prompt tuning, and prefix tuning alter the processing of dense and mixture-of-experts language models. Our analysis shows that the location of the ada

title: Lightweight but Linguistically Fair? Quantisation Robustness across Bavarian, German, and English
authors: Jophin John, Michael Hoffmann, Piroska Lendvai et al.
abstract: Post-training quantisation reduces the memory cost of large language models, but it remains unclear whether compression preserves language skills of regional varieties as reliably as their standard-language counterparts. We study this question for Bavarian, Standard German, and English using BAVGROUND, a multiple-choice benchmark, where 206 source questions are aligned across all three languages. title: Probing the Geometry of Color Representations in Multilingual Language Models
authors: Pablo Loyola, Edison Marrese-Taylor, Andrés Hoyos-Idrobo
abstract: Do multilingual language models learn a universal internal geometry for color, and is it perceptually grounded or primarily linguistic? We decompose color representations into two geometric axes: (P1) alignment to perceptual color space, and (P2) cross-lingual symmetry. Analyzing layerwise embeddings across models and multilingual datasets, we find that perceptual grounding is weak: alignment to CIE-LAB peaks in intermediate layers, then collapses toward output layers. title: Claim Framing as a Driver of LLM Sycophancy
authors: Jean Seo, Pepa Atanasova, Isabelle Augenstein
abstract: Sycophancy in Large Language Models, the tendency to align responses with user preferences over ground truth, has largely been studied using questions without a clear ground truth and with a single, plainly stated user opinion. We present a systematic study of which framings of a user's claim trigger sycophancy in factual question answering, where every answer is objectively verifiable without extra context. title: From Agents to Edges: Paired Optimization for Multi-Agent Collaboration
authors: Feng Lin, Xiaotian Yu, Yifan Yang et al.
abstract: Strong individual agents do not guarantee effective collaboration. Communication must align what one agent conveys with how another interprets and uses it. This dependency makes the communication edge a natural unit of optimization. We introduce Paired Automated Communication Optimization (PACO), which jointly optimizes the instructions at both ends of each edge and their shared communication convention in systems built on black-box language models. PACO keeps model weights, agent roles, and wor

title: Text-Only vs. Image-Aware VLM Judges for Manga Translation Evaluation
authors: Subaru Kimura, Jun Suzuki
abstract: In manga translation, visual context outside speech-bubble text, including speaker identities, referents, and scene tone, is depicted in page images, making it natural to refer to images during translation evaluation. However, most conventional manga translation evaluations rely solely on text-only automatic metrics, leaving the impact of image input insufficiently explored. title: DriveWLA: Unifying Future Dynamics and Scene Semantics through World-Language-Action Modeling for Autonomous Driving
authors: Shuzheng Wang, Haoxuan Li, Shengzhen Li et al.
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and world models have demonstrated strong capabilities in semantic understanding and future scene evolution for autonomous driving. However, effectively integrating both capabilities for trajectory generation remains challenging. In this work, we propose DriveWLA, a unified World-Language-Action model based on Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) that jointly models semantic understanding, future scene dynamics, and trajectory generation. DriveWLA consists of three experts

title: Visual Dependence Does Not Imply Answerability: A Systematic Analysis of Answerability Signals in Frozen InstructBLIP
authors: Minjun Kim, Hyunmin Song, Changwon Lim
abstract: Visual question answering models often produce plausible responses even when the available visual evidence is insufficient to support a valid answer. Although prior work has introduced benchmarks and abstention mechanisms for unanswerable visual questions, it remains unclear which signals derived from a frozen vision-language model reliably indicate answerability on unseen image-question pairs. title: RoTA-Bench: Evaluating 3D Spatial Reasoning through Interactive Projection Alignment
authors: Qingchuan Ma, Yuexiao Ma, Xiang Meng et al.
abstract: Can vision-language models turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise action? This requires inferring object geometry, anticipating the effects of rotation, and refining actions through visual feedback. We introduce RoTA-Bench to evaluate these abilities through interactive 3D-to-2D projection alignment. title: Read the Room Before Your Model Generates
authors: Muyao Kong, Zhihao Lin
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generally rely on sampling temperature to regulate the amount of randomness in their outputs. Mainstream methods for selecting temperature typically involve fixed, heuristic global settings and context or token-level calibration, rather than a geometrically interpretable representation of the communicative scenario. In this work, we introduce a simple and interpretable temperature selection framework, the \textbf{Scenario-Actor}, which adapts decoding to the inferred

title: Back-Translation Still Matters: Leveraging Monolingual Data for Low-Resource Machine Translation with LLMs
authors: Divyanshu Bathla, Parag Singla, Jitin Singla
abstract: Pre-trained Large Language Model (LLMs) are effective on many tasks in zero-shot and few-shot settings. For machine translation of low-resource languages, the obvious options are few-shot prompting and fine-tuning on a small parallel set. We ask: what if moderate amounts of low-resource monolingual data are also available? title: SolBehave: Evaluating the Behavioural Correctness of LLM-Generated Smart Contracts
authors: Giovanni Pio Delvecchio, Stefano Fantazzini, Giacomo Frisoni et al.
abstract: Large language models increasingly generate Solidity smart contracts that, once deployed, can never be patched, making a single latent fault permanent and exploitable. Yet current evaluations mostly ask only whether generated code compiles. We introduce SolBehave, a benchmark for evaluating the correctness of model-generated contracts at scale, moving beyond ad hoc unit tests. Across 250 real, reproducible Ethereum contracts, we apply three complementary tests of behavioural fidelity: differenti

title: Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models
authors: Jie Chi, Zakaria Aldeneh, Masha Fedzechkina et al.
abstract: Code-switching (CS), the alternation between languages within an utterance, is common in multilingual speech but underrepresented in pretraining corpora. Increasing CS coverage requires finding relevant utterances in large speech collections so that they can be included in training data. One way to find such utterances is to transcribe the speech and detect language alternation in the text, but this depends on obtaining accurate multilingual transcriptions. We propose a lightweight method that d

title: From Relation-Specific Heads to Shared Interventions: Contextual Entrainment in Language Models
authors: Jinghan Zheng, Jiajun Shi
abstract: Large language models rely on prompt context to perform in-context learning, follow formats, and adapt to local evidence. This ability, however, also raises a robustness concern: models may reuse irrelevant tokens from earlier context when answering a later query. Prior work identifies this behavior as contextual entrainment and finds attention heads whose ablation reduces it, arguing that these heads are largely task- or relation-specific. But are the mechanisms behind contextual entrainment tr

title: From Hindsight to Foresight: Dissecting Clinical Evidence Acquisition in Large Language Models
authors: Ziyang Ling
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often diagnose full sight, static clinical cases well yet struggle in foresight, dynamic diagnosis. Prior work has improved this limitation by quantifying the information models acquire and by developing stronger follow-up strategies to improve diagnostic accuracy. In contrast, we introduce a distinctive hindsight to systematically dissect why LLMs fail to acquire diagnostically critical evidence, tracing the failure from evidence identification, utilization and down

title: ACCRUE: Continual Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Robot Foundation Models
authors: Changyeon Kim, Kimin Lee, Yashraj Narang et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves robot foundation models (RFMs) beyond their demonstrations, but real-world deployment demands more: learning new tasks efficiently while retaining previously acquired behaviors. Existing continual RL methods on top of VLAs mitigate forgetting but rely on on-policy updates with limited forward transfer, whereas off-policy methods improve single-task sample efficiency without addressing learner persistence across tasks. We propose ACCRUE, a contin

title: The Many Morals of AI: The cautionary bias of North American news narratives in global perspective
authors: Andrew Piper, Edie Pearman
abstract: The stories told about artificial intelligence (AI) play a central role in shaping public understanding, policy debates, and expectations about technological change. News media are especially influential in this process. Using a cross-regional corpus of 12,924 English-language news articles about AI published since 2022, we examine how storytelling about AI varies across media systems in four regions: North America, China, India, and the Middle East. Leveraging large language models, we extract

title: Rethinking Quality in Large Language Model Routing: Security-Conditioned Model-and-Budget Selection
authors: Yichi Zhang, Zhenxiang Huang, Yuyang Zhang et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) routers reduce serving cost by choosing which model to call and how many output tokens to grant it for each query. Existing routers rank model-budget actions using a single quality metric. This does not work for mixed workloads. For ordinary queries, a good answer is correct and useful (utility); for security-sensitive queries, a good answer refuses harmful requests or resists malicious instructions (security). These two objectives prefer different models and budgets.

title: A Global View of How LLMs Value Human Time
authors: Yifan He, Sofie Goethals, Manon Reusens et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as personal assistants; however, little is known about how they capture national-level preferences on a global scale. Given that "time" is a universal and representative concept, we examine LLMs' time preferences by varying only users' country and measuring the compensation LLMs deem appropriate for a 60-minute appointment delay. We then compare LLMs' responses with GDP per capita on Purchasing Power Parity (GDP_PPP), Mean Income, and a literature-ba

title: The Smart Buildings Challenge: Learning Foundation Models for Real-World Optimization at Scale
authors: Judah Goldfeder, Ayush Rai, Philippe M. Wyder et al.
abstract: Buildings cause nearly 40\% of carbon emissions in the US. Of total building emissions, HVAC systems are responsible for approximately 40-60\% and account for 15\% of global energy consumption. Despite advances in artificial intelligence, most buildings still operate as inefficiently as they did decades ago. Building optimization, perhaps more so than any other optimization problem, has enormous potential for Machine Learning (ML) driven impact on climate change, in both the short and long term.

title: How Well Do LLMs Perform in Peer Review? Evidence from Finance and Accounting
authors: Hai Lu, Yichen Luo, Luping Yu
abstract: Referees increasingly use large language models (LLMs), while finance and accounting journals disagree about whether to allow it. We ask which part of a referee's job the models can do. GPT-4o, whose training data end before the 2024 conference season, referees the papers presented at the 2024 AFA and NBER finance meetings, and we compare its verdicts with publication in the top-three finance journals over the next two years. Papers the model scores one standard deviation higher are 44\% more li

title: FedGraph: Defending Federated Large Language Model Fine-Tuning Against Backdoor Attacks via Graph-Based Aggregation
authors: Xi Chen, Chunyi Zhou, Rui Zeng et al.
abstract: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) allows multiple clients to collaboratively adapt models without sharing raw data, offering strong privacy benefits. However, this setting is highly vulnerable to backdoor attacks, in which malicious clients manipulate their updates to induce targeted behaviors while maintaining normal performance on benign inputs. In this work, we make a key observation specific to federated LLM fine-tuning: malicious clients tend to exhibit strong consistenc

title: PRISM: Calibrating Black-Box Judges with Counterfactual Probes
authors: Kakei Yamamoto, So Kuroki
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as judges to reduce reliance on costly human evaluation, yet their scores can systematically disagree with human judgments. We ask whether responses to an explicitly imposed evaluative bias can help correct a judge's implicit scoring biases. We introduce PRISM (Probe-based Residual Inference of Scoring Misalignment), which holds the evaluated content fixed and measures score changes when attributes are emphasized or de-emphasized. A local sensitivity m

title: ABot-ER: Unified Embodied Reasoning through Agentic Data-Model Co-Evolution
authors: Qiuyu Ding, Heng-Da Xu, Changda Xia et al.
abstract: We introduce \textbf{ABot Embodied Reasoning (ABot-ER)}, a unified embodied reasoning foundation model that breaks the tension between breadth and depth in embodied reasoning. Embodied intelligence demands the joint mastery of perception, planning, and execution, yet reconciling generality with specialization across this spectrum remains an open challenge. Within a single unified model, ABot-ER commands specialist-level depth across all three competencies, spanning spatial, scene, and temporal r

title: PAINT: A Framework for Multilingual Pain Representation from Medical Licensing Exams to Real-World Clinical Texts
authors: Boya Zhang, Yuanchao Ma, Jiageng Wu et al.
abstract: Pain is one of the most common and clinically important symptoms, reflecting disease onset, progression, and treatment response. However, pain is difficult to accurately capture and interpret from medical text, as its expression varies across languages, documentation types, and patient demographics, and is often embedded in terminology, negation, temporality, and contextual descriptions. Existing pain-related studies remain largely monolingual or limited to narrow clinical settings. In this stud

title: Are We Testing Too Much? A Survey of Benchmark Compression for Efficient Evaluation of Large Language Models
authors: Guoming Ling, Yupei Lin, Zhongzhan Huang et al.
abstract: Benchmarks are essential for evaluating and improving large language models (LLMs). Yet many widely used benchmarks are redundant, making evaluation unnecessarily expensive. Benchmark compression lowers this cost by estimating full-benchmark scores and rankings from a partial evaluation. Research in this area has grown rapidly since 2024, but to our knowledge no survey has systematically organized its methods and findings.
